questions.prompt: `CountingSortByAge` is the stable, cumulative-count version. In what order are the employees after this call?
options: Sana (25), Riya (25), Vikram (28), Karan (30), Aman (30)
Riya (25), Sana (25), Vikram (28), Aman (30), Karan (30)
Riya (25), Sana (25), Vikram (28), Karan (30), Aman (30)
Aman (30), Karan (30), Vikram (28), Riya (25), Sana (25)

source.section: Worked example: sorting objects by a key

questions.prompt: In the stable counting sort, Step 3 walks the input from right to left. Why?
options: It makes the algorithm run in O(n) instead of O(n + k)
It avoids an index-out-of-range error on the first element
Cumulative counts point at the last valid slot for each value, so filling from the right keeps equal elements in their original order
It lets the sort write directly into `arr` without an `output` array
questions.explanation: After Step 2 each count is the last output slot for that value. Placing elements from the right and decrementing the count puts the last tie in the last slot, which preserves original order.

questions.prompt: You only need to sort a plain `int[]`. Which counting-sort version does the lesson recommend, and why?
options: The simple version, because both produce identical output for plain integers and it is easier to read
The stable version, because the simple version gives wrong output for duplicates
The stable version, because it is asymptotically faster
Neither; counting sort cannot sort negative integers
questions.explanation: For plain integers a `3` is indistinguishable from any other `3`, so stability is invisible and both versions give the same result. The stable version matters when sorting objects by a key.

questions.prompt: When does the lesson call counting sort impractical?
options: When the input contains duplicate values
When the input is already sorted
When the array has more than a few thousand elements
When the value range `k` is very large compared with `n`, such as 10 numbers with values up to 10⁹
questions.explanation: Counting sort costs O(n + k) time and space, so a huge range wastes memory and time. It shines on bounded ranges such as ages 0-120 or scores 0-100.

questions.prompt: How does radix sort process the numbers?
options: Digit by digit from the most significant digit, using quicksort on each digit
By comparing whole numbers pairwise, like merge sort
Digit by digit from the least significant digit, using a stable sort such as counting sort on each digit
By distributing numbers into buckets by value range and sorting each bucket
questions.explanation: Radix sort goes from the least significant to the most significant digit and uses a stable per-digit sort (typically counting sort), so it needs no comparisons at all.

questions.prompt: Bucket sort is near-linear on uniformly distributed input. When does it degrade to O(n²)?
options: When the data is skewed or clustered, so most elements land in one bucket
When the input is already sorted
When there are more buckets than elements
When the values are floats instead of integers
questions.explanation: The worst case is all elements in one bucket, where sorting that single bucket dominates. Bucket sort needs prior knowledge of the data's distribution and range to work well.
